item.title: Treaty Feasibility & Cost Analysis
item.description: Previous treaties failed because they ran on guilt. Guilt has terrible fuel efficiency. This one runs on greed, which is (regrettably) humanity's only reliable fuel source.

item.title: Campaign Budget: The Legal Bribery Machine
Recruitment & Propaganda Plan
item.description: You want to end war and disease but don't have a nonprofit, a bank account, or anything to offer anyone. Here's how to recruit 100,000 humans before you have anything except an argument. It's a Kickstarter where the reward tier is 'possibly not dying,' which is the most compelling crowdfunding offer in history.

item.title: Building Your AI Coordination Army
item.description: How to build and deploy autonomous AI agents that coordinate millions of people fighting the War on Disease.

item.title: Global Referendum Strategy
item.description: Humanity downloaded TikTok over 4 billion times to watch strangers twerk. Getting 280 million people to click 'yes' on not dying should be easier. Here's how, with math.

item.title: Legal Architecture
item.description: Bribing politicians is illegal unless you call it 'lobbying' or 'campaign contributions.' Then it's protected speech. Here's the legal architecture for saving humanity using your own ridiculous laws.

item.title: Why Every Nonprofit Should Support a 1% treaty
item.description: Nonprofits fighting disease currently compete for the same shrinking pile of donor money. A 1% treaty creates $27.2 billion in new funding. Here's how to get every health nonprofit to stop fighting over crumbs and start fighting for the bakery.

item.title: Frequently Asked Objections
item.description: Fun facts for those reasonably skeptical of spending 1% more on helping sick people than killing them.

item.title: The Roadmap to End War and Disease
item.description: Here are the exact steps from incorporating a nonprofit to ratifying an international treaty, with a budget for every phase.

Redirect of military spending and it drops to , preventing at the cost-effectiveness of anti-malaria bed nets. The whole thing costs less per year to run than Halloween costumes for dogs. But sure, take your time.

item.title: Peace Dividend
item.description: Your government spends more on camouflage paint than on curing Alzheimer''s. Move 1% of the bomb budget to medicine: $27.2 billion for clinical trials, plus $114 billion saved by slightly fewer explosions. The worst-case scenario is still the largest increase in medical research in history.

item.title: Financial Plan
item.description: Invest $1B. Pass a treaty. Manage $27.2B/year forever. 80% cures diseases, 10% pays investors, 10% keeps politicians obedient. Three pillars, no committees, no generosity required.

item.title: Incentive Alignment Bonds
item.description: War bonds, but backwards. Your grandparents funded WW2 at roughly 3% returns. You fund disease eradication at 272%. Same structure, fewer Nazis, better spreadsheet.

item.title: Solution Overview
item.description: How to Build Systems That Don't Suck

item.title: The Proof: Overview
item.description: This Already Works - Pragmatic trials prove efficiency. History proves every component. Switzerland, war bonds, landmines, the 3.5% rule, and Wall Street's craziest bets all prove humans can accidentally do smart things when properly motivated.

item.title: The Two Futures
item.description: Two timelines diverge from this moment. One ends in extinction, the other in transcendence. The only difference is a 1% budget reallocation.

item.title: Real-World Evidence Historical Success (Pre-1962)
item.description: How decentralized physician trials from 1883-1962 achieved 4 years/decade life expectancy gains, and what happened when the 1962 regulations replaced them with industry-controlled trials

item.title: The Oxford RECOVERY Trial
item.description: Proof that decentralized pragmatic trials reduce costs by 82X while saving millions of lives

item.title: The Untapped Therapeutic Frontier
item.description: There are 9.5 million possible drug-disease combinations. You've tested 32,500. That's like searching for your keys in 0.34% of your house and declaring them lost. The other 99.7% is sitting right there, untested, because paperwork.

item.title: The Cost of Disease
item.description: The annual bill for letting your bodies fall apart. It's more than all the money on Earth, which is impressive in a terrible way.

item.title: Problem Overview
item.description: Humanity's spectacular failure at prioritizing not dying

item.title: Aligning Incentives
item.description: Pharmaceutical companies make more money treating you forever than curing you once. Defense contractors earn $1,425 per lobbying dollar. This chapter redesigns the profit motive so curing disease pays better than causing it. Capitalism, but pointed at the right target.

item.title: A Decentralized Framework for Drug Assessment
item.description: It costs $41,000 per patient to test a drug. Oxford proved you can do it for $500. This framework lets every patient on Earth join clinical trials, cuts costs over 40x, and turns medical records into the largest drug-testing dataset in history. The only losers are the diseases.

item.title: Wishocracy
item.description: How to spend $27.2 billion a year on curing disease without it getting stolen by lobbyists, committees, and people whose main qualification is seniority. Democracy, but designed by someone who actually wanted it to work.

item.title: Decentralized Institutes of Health
item.description: You''ve been fighting disease like a cat fights a laser pointer: lots of energy, no coordination, nothing caught. This is the plan to make curing disease the most profitable thing every hospital, pharma company, and researcher can do, so they do it by accident while trying to get rich.

item.title: You Are a Meat Robot
item.description: You can 3D-print a windpipe, reprogram skin cells into brain cells, and restore vision with a single injection. Then you went back to mostly not doing any of that. Fascinating.

item.title: Wishonia
item.description: On one planet, citizens allocate the budget directly, lobbyists don't exist, and disease was eradicated 4,000 years ago. It uses the same technology you have. The difference is they pointed it at biology instead of each other.

item.title: A 1% Treaty
item.description: You have enough nuclear weapons to kill everyone 13 times. Here's how to settle for 12.87 times and use the savings on medicine. Controversial, apparently.

item.title: Unrepresentative Democracy
item.description: Princeton proved that public opinion has zero effect on U.S. policy. Corporations spend $4.4 billion on lobbying and get an 18:1 return. Your vote is worth $0.00017. Here's how to make the math work for medicine instead of missiles.

item.title: How Central Banks Fund Your Death
item.description: Every fiat currency in history has been devalued to fund wars nobody voted for. Your savings lose value each year to pay for bombs you didn't order. Here's how central banks quietly tax you to fund the war machine, and what to do about it.

item.title: NIH Fails to Institute Health
item.description: The National Institutes of Health spends 96.7% of its budget on everything except testing whether drugs work in humans. It's like a fire department that spends 96.7% of its budget on fire-themed calendars and 3.3% on water.

item.title: The Cost of War
item.description: Quantifying Human Idiocy - A precise accounting of what humans spend to destroy themselves, with numbers that would make a statistician weep.

item.title: The FDA Is Unsafe and Ineffective
item.description: Dying patients can't access drugs that already passed every safety test. They also can't join the trials testing those drugs. They can, however, die. Nobody blocks that.

item.title: The Cautionary Tale of Moronia
item.description: A planet had every tool needed to cure disease and chose to build weapons instead. They went extinct. Their last words were 'but the economy.' This is a bedtime story for civilizations that can't do math.

item.title: Genetic Slavery
item.description: You're running 200,000-year-old software on modern hardware. Your brain was designed for running from lions; now it runs from emails, craves sugar that's everywhere, fears strangers it needs to cooperate with, and builds nuclear weapons using the same instinct that once made it good at throwing rocks.
